title: What Did New Horizons Discover Inside Pluto's Frozen Heart?
description:
Why Pluto's Frozen Heart Has Zero Craters

Across Pluto's horizon, what would you see on the bright western half of its icy heart? A frozen nitrogen glacier about 1,000 kilometres (600 miles) wide — larger than Texas and Oklahoma combined — with zero craters. On 13 and 14 July 2015, NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew within 12,500 kilometres (7,800 miles) of Pluto, 39 times farther from the Sun than Earth at −232 degrees Celsius (−387 degrees Fahrenheit), and solved that mystery.

Sources: NASA Science, Pluto Facts — 39 AU average distance, −232 °C (−387 °F) average temperature, craters up to 260 km (162 miles) across elsewhere on Pluto, and crater-free convecting nitrogen plains (https://science.nasa.gov/dwarf-planets/pluto/facts/) · NASA Science, New Horizons Mission — 13–14 July 2015 Pluto flyby within 12,500 km (7,800 miles) and ~1,000 km (600-mile) Sputnik Planitia nitrogen glacier (https://science.nasa.gov/mission/new-horizons/) · NASA Science News (5 August 2026, Alan Stern et al.) — Sputnik Planitia frozen nitrogen glacier larger than Texas and Oklahoma combined (https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/science-news/2026/08/05/nasas-new-horizons-finds-evidence-of-recent-liquid-on-plutos-surface/).

Pictures: NASA/JHUAPL/SwRI New Horizons LORRI and Ralph/MVIC imagery (14 July 2015 flyby sequence, PIA20291, PIA20726, PIA20007, PIA19952, PIA20534, PIA20198, PIA20038, PIA20732, PIA19936) and NASA Blue Marble Earth (PIA18033) alongside original animated explainers, with AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Southwest Research Institute (New Horizons, 14 July 2015 LORRI flyby sequence, PIA20291, PIA20726, PIA20007, PIA19952, PIA20534, PIA20198, PIA20038, PIA20732, PIA19936); NASA Goddard Space Flight Center/Reto Stöckli (Blue Marble Earth, PIA18033).
